Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Abdullah Bozkurt/Stockholm Turkey is developing a sprawling rocket launch facility on Somalia’s Indian Ocean coast that is publicly presented as a civilian spaceport for commercial satellite launches but is also emerging as a potential testing ground for the country’s expanding long-range ballistic missile arsenal, according to Turkish government documents, parliamentary testimony and reports on Ankara’s enhanced military hardware acquisition plans. An examination of financial records published by the Turkish Space Agency (Türkiye Uzay Ajansı, TUA) reveals that the government allocated 2.1 billion Turkish lira, equivalent to approximately $42 million at November 2026 exchange rates, for transfer to the Defense Industry Support Fund under the country’s national space access and spaceport program. The financial arrangement, disclosed in a footnote to the agency’s 2026 performance program, establishes an official connection between Turkey’s civilian space ambitions and the financial mechanism used to support its military and its defense industry. The documents do not specify how much of the allocation, if any, has been spent on the construction of the Somali facility or on missile-related infrastructure. The project, estimated in media reports to cost approximately $350 million, is taking shape near the coastal town of Warsheikh, about 70 kilometers north of Mogadishu. The planned development covers an area reportedly measuring about 900 square kilometers, giving Turkey access to a substantial stretch of territory for launching rockets toward the Indian Ocean. Its location is critical to both the civilian and potential military dimensions of the project. Somalia’s proximity to the equator offers advantages for putting satellites into orbit, while the vast expanse of the Indian Ocean provides a geographically convenient corridor for long-range missile trials, reducing the risk of rocket debris falling on densely populated areas or neighboring countries. The clearest documentary indication of the project’s connection to the Turkish military appears in TUA’s official 2026 Performance Program, published on the agency’s website. The detail was buried in a footnote on page 23 that said an additional 2.1 billion lira was incorporated into the agency’s 2025 budget under the National Space Program’s Uzaya Erişim ve Uzay Limanı (Access to Space and Spaceport) activity. The Turkish Space Agency’s 2026 Performance Program reveals a 2.1 billion lira ($42 million) allocation for transfer to the Defense Industry Support Fund under its spaceport program, highlighting a financial link between Turkey’s civilian space ambitions and its defense industry: The document specifies that the allocation was intended for transfer to the Savunma Sanayii Destekleme Fonu (Defense Industry Support Fund, SSDF), citing legislation published in the Official Gazette on July 24, 2025, issue No. 32965. The fund is a vital financing instrument for Turkey’s military-industrial programs and is institutionally distinct from the Turkish Armed Forces’ operational budget. It supports the development and procurement of defense technologies, including strategically significant domestic capabilities. The use of this financing mechanism for a program publicly promoted around satellite launches raises questions about the division of responsibilities between TUA and Turkey’s defense establishment, particularly the Presidency of the Defense Industry (SSB) which reports directly to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. The same performance program puts TUA’s overall 2025 budget at approximately 4.58 billion lira, with a 2026 budget of 5.92 billion lira. In his introduction to the program, Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır said the planned spaceport was intended to support Turkey’s independent access to space and strategic launches. The description reinforces the government’s emphasis on strategic autonomy, without defining the military or civilian status of individual future launches. The connection between Turkey’s space ambitions and its military-industrial establishment predates the construction of the Somali facility. TUA’s 2022 Activity Report reveals that the agency began an extensive assessment in 2021 under the National Space Program to study future launch vehicles, payloads, orbital requirements and rocket launch facilities. Four working groups were established to examine payloads, launch vehicles, innovative propulsion and component technologies and launch-base infrastructure. On February 22, 2022, TUA held a meeting to present the findings of its Independent Access to Space and Spaceport Analysis Report. Among the organizations invited were leading Turkish defense contractors Roketsan, ASELSAN, Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAŞ/TAI), STM and DeltaV, together with TÜBİTAK SAGE, TÜBİTAK UZAY, TÜRKSAT and other aerospace companies. The agency said the resulting analysis was distributed to relevant stakeholders. It was kept confidential from public scrutiny. Turkey’s GÖKTÜRK-2, a domestically developed Earth observation and reconnaissance satellite designed to provide high-resolution imagery for civilian and military applications, is launched into orbit aboard a Chinese Long March rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in China on December 18, 2012. The involvement of Roketsan is particularly significant. The company is a major developer of Turkish rocket and missile systems, including the Tayfun ballistic missile family. It also works on technologies intended to provide Turkey with independent satellite-launch capabilities. TUA’s website identifies Roketsan as the contractor selected under a 2018 agreement with the Presidency of the Defense Industry for the Micro Satellite Launch System, known by its Turkish abbreviation MUFS. The program aims to develop the ability to put satellites weighing up to 100 kilograms into low Earth orbit at altitudes of at least 400 kilometers. It also envisages the development of domestic infrastructure for manufacturing, testing and launching space vehicles. Although satellite-launch vehicles and ballistic missiles serve different purposes, some of their underlying technologies overlap, particularly rocket propulsion, structural materials, guidance and control and testing infrastructure. The overlap means that investment in satellite-launch technology can also strengthen the industrial capabilities needed for sophisticated missile systems. Further evidence of the facility’s anticipated use by Turkish defense contractors emerged in December 2025 when Selçuk Bayraktar, chairman of drone manufacturer Baykar and son-in-law of President Erdogan, discussed the Somali project at a technology event in Istanbul. Bayraktar said the state had begun construction of the launch facility and specifically identified Roketsan as a prospective user. He also said he hoped to use the site for launch vehicles developed by his own aerospace ventures. His remarks identified a direct prospective role for Roketsan at the Somali facility, going beyond its participation in the earlier feasibility studies. Turkey’s then-defense minister Hulusi Akar examines the İMECE satellite, the country’s first domestically developed high-resolution Earth observation satellite, during a visit on June 4, 2020, as officials completed the assembly of its final components ahead of testing. The satellite was designed for civilian and military reconnaissance applications. Turkey’s search for an overseas launch facility is closely connected to the geographical limitations it faces in developing both an independent space program and longer-range missiles. Launching spacecraft eastward from a location close to the equator can improve the efficiency of reaching certain orbits by taking advantage of the Earth’s rotation. Such launches also require large safety zones to accommodate the possibility of falling rocket components. Turkey’s own geography creates complications. To its north lies the Black Sea, bordered by Russia, Ukraine and other countries, while its southern approaches involve the Mediterranean, Cyprus and densely trafficked air and maritime routes. A launch site facing the Indian Ocean offers a potentially much larger testing corridor. President Erdogan had previously announced plans to increase Turkey’s inventory of missiles with ranges of around 800 kilometers while accelerating work on systems capable of reaching 2,000 kilometers. Reports suggested that Turkey is working on testing missiles with a range of some 6,000 kilometers as well. The Somali site could provide testing opportunities for those programs, although there is no publicly established evidence that particular missile systems have been assigned to launches from Warsheikh. According to an account published by the state-run Anadolu news agency on January 1, 2026, the Somali project is being developed in three phases, with the initial focus on establishing launch infrastructure and the subsequent ambition of offering commercial services. The envisioned facility would initially support Turkish satellites and eventually serve foreign customers seeking access to low Earth orbit and other orbital destinations. The government also expects the project to stimulate the development of domestic rocket engines, propulsion technologies, advanced materials, avionics and ground-support systems. Such programs routinely involve technologies relevant to military communications, reconnaissance and navigation, even when launch services are sold commercially. Turkey is believed to have been trying to combine its expanding ballistic missile ambitions under the pretext of developing a spaceport in Somalia. Ankara has not publicly disclosed a comprehensive operational framework separating the site’s civilian satellite-launch activities from any military testing arrangements. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan meets with Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud at the Presidential Dolmabahçe Office in Istanbul on April 16, 2026. The government provided a fresh confirmation of the project’s progress during a November 2, 2026, hearing of the Turkish Parliament’s Planning and Budget Committee. Presenting the Industry and Technology Ministry’s 2027 budget, Minister Kacır said the government was moving toward the capability to launch Turkish satellites using domestically developed rockets. He specifically referred to construction of the Somali spaceport as a central element of this ambition. The minister said the facility would give Turkey independent access to space and enable it to obtain a larger share of the global space economy. He carefully avoided making any reference to the military aspect of the project. His remarks nevertheless confirmed that the Somali facility has advanced beyond an initial proposal and forms part of Turkey’s active national space strategy. The Turkish government also has ambitions to deploy space-based systems that could support intelligence collection, communications and navigation, capabilities of obvious interest to the country’s military establishment. Another potentially important development appears in a June 26, 2026, announcement published by TUA. The agency disclosed that it had hosted a meeting involving the ambassadors of Somalia and Qatar in Ankara to discuss cooperation in space-related activities. The Somali ambassador, Fathudin Ali Mohamed, and Qatari Ambassador Faisal bin Abdulla Al-Henzab attended the meeting, which focused on access to space, space systems, opportunities for cooperation and regional partnerships. According to the agency, participants also considered ways to strengthen exchanges of knowledge, experience and technology. Personnel from the Somali National Army’s 5th Eagle Battalion participate in infiltration training conducted by Turkey’s 1st Airborne and Commando Brigade Command, as announced by the Turkish Ministry of Defense on October 16, 2026. The exercise highlights Turkey’s continuing role in training and strengthening Somalia’s military forces. Although the announcement did not specifically identify the Somali launch complex as the subject of a trilateral agreement, the presence of both countries at a meeting devoted to space access is noteworthy. Qatar is an important strategic partner of Erdogan’s government, with extensive defense and economic ties to Turkey, including defense-industry cooperation. While Turkey provides muscle and technology to military projects, Qatar is poised to bankroll such ambitious projects in Turkey. The spaceport is being established against the background of Turkey’s extensive military, economic and political involvement in Somalia. Ankara has substantially expanded its presence in the country since Erdogan’s visit to Mogadishu in 2011, building relationships across defense cooperation, infrastructure, energy, education and government institutions. Turkey opened a major overseas military training facility in Mogadishu in 2017. Commonly known as TURKSOM, the installation serves as a center for training Somali military personnel and represents one of Turkey’s most important military commitments outside its immediate region. The facility, reportedly established at a cost of around $50 million, has the capacity to train thousands of Somali soldiers. Turkey and Somalia have subsequently concluded additional defense and maritime security agreements, expanding Ankara’s role in helping protect Somali territorial waters and supporting Somali security institutions.In July 2024 the Turkish Parliament approved a presidential motion authorizing the deployment of Turkish naval forces to Somalia under the countries’ defense cooperation arrangements. Turkey’s expanding security role has coincided with growing commercial interests, including infrastructure management and prospective hydrocarbon exploration. Turkish companies have a significant presence in the management of Mogadishu’s airport and seaport, while Ankara has also pursued agreements involving offshore and onshore energy exploration. The spaceport would add another strategically important installation to this network, potentially allowing Turkey to combine military training, maritime security, aerospace technology and launch operations within a single partner country. The financial structure of the project remains largely undisclosed. Although TUA’s performance program identifies a 2.1 billion lira allocation associated with a transfer to the Defense Industry Support Fund, the agency has not established in the reviewed documents which contracts were financed through that mechanism or whether the money was spent directly on the Warsheikh site. Similarly, the frequently reported $350 million construction estimate has not been reconciled with a publicly available, comprehensive project budget. There are also unanswered questions about the companies responsible for building the complex. Turkey’s ambassador to Somalia, Ferhat Alkan, and TURKSOM military base commander Maj. Gen. Sabahattin Kalkan, accompanied by a Turkish delegation, visit Warsheikh in Somalia’s Middle Shabelle region to inspect the site of a Turkish-developed satellite launch facility. The October 5, 2026, visit comes amid Ankara’s expanding military and commercial presence in Somalia, including plans for a new port, special economic zone and industrial facilities near Warsheikh. Turkey’s Albayrak Group, a conglomerate with considerable business interests in Somalia and close ties to President Erdogan, has been mentioned in reports concerning visits by Turkish delegations to the spaceport construction site. Ahmet Sami İşler, the group’s general manager in Somalia and chairman of the Turkey–Somalia Business Council, reportedly briefed a visiting delegation on the project. The Albayrak Group has longstanding ties to Erdogan’s government and has supported political Islamist initiatives in Turkey and abroad. Its flagship media outlet, the Islamist Yeni Şafak daily, has been a staunch supporter of Erdogan and his political Islamist agenda, consistently promoting his government’s policies and ideological positions. The government’s own statements more clearly identify Roketsan as a prospective user of the facility, while TUA’s earlier planning documents show the involvement of numerous other Turkish defense and aerospace organizations. Satellite launch vehicles and ballistic missiles rely on some common engineering disciplines, including propulsion, aerodynamics, structural design, navigation and control. Investment in one field can therefore provide technical benefits to the other. The involvement of the Presidency of the Defense Industry and companies such as Roketsan reinforces the strategic importance of this technological convergence. The Erdogan government has consistently promoted domestic defense production and technological independence as central pillars of Turkey’s national security strategy. The Somali spaceport appears to fit into this broader strategy, combining ambitions to compete in the international space industry with the development of strategically sensitive technologies. For now, however, it remains unclear how much of the facility’s infrastructure, financing and operational capacity will ultimately be devoted to advancing Turkey’s military missile program. somalia.content: The UN's exit from Somalia's political arena: What comes next? - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION The UN's exit from Somalia's political arena: What comes next? Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Hussein Shegow Mohamed Sunday November 8, 2026 After more than three decades, the United Nations political mission in Somalia closes today. The country asked for it. The harder question is whether its institutions are ready. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) concludes its mandate on 31 October 2026. On October 31, 2026, the UN ends its political mission in Somalia. A ceremony was held in Mogadishu earlier that week to commemorate the conclusion of 13 years of work that began with the creation of UNSOM in 2013. If you go back a little further, the story is older. In 1995, a political office was established by the UN for Somalia. Thus, it is not the end of a single mission when the doors close. It's the end of a long-standing habit. People are already asking what happens now. It's a fair question, and I don't think the honest answer is either "everything will be fine" or "the country will fall apart." advertisements Let's begin with something that is frequently overlooked. This was requested by Somalia. The foreign minister requested in a letter to the Security Council in May 2024 that the mission's mandate expire in October of that same year. Later, Mogadishu consented to a more gradual departure, and the Council unanimously approved a two-year transition that would conclude on October 31, 2026, with the mission being renamed UNTMIS. Its responsibilities were supposed to be transferred to Somali institutions and the remaining UN agencies. And they do remain. After the mandate expires, the UN has stated that it will continue to support Somalia. Humanitarian organizations, development initiatives, clinic staff, and food distributors all continue to exist. The political office, which consisted of a small team of advisors and diplomats tasked with reaching out to all parties, negotiating agreements, and documenting issues, disappears. That final point, in my opinion, is more important than we realize. Anyone who has followed Somali politics is aware of how frequently the real struggle is not with Al-Shabaab but rather between Mogadishu and the federal member states over issues like elections, the constitution, and power. Someone had to sit in the middle and be trusted by both parties when those discussions broke down in the past. Although it wasn't flawless, the UN was typically trusted enough to bring people together. Now, who does that? The Union of Africa? adjacent governments? The Gulf states, Turkey? Everyone in the room is aware of their shared interests in Somalia. An exit works when local institutions are already strong enough to carry the load, and it hurts when the exit date arrives before they are. Lessons from Liberia Examining another nation that experienced a similar situation is beneficial. I keep thinking about Liberia as an example. After fifteen years, UNMIL, the UN peacekeeping force stationed there, came to an end in March 2018. Liberia had recently accomplished something that many had doubted it could: in 2017, a president peacefully transferred power to a successor through an election, something that hadn't happened in decades. The exit was hailed as evidence of the nation's maturity. And it had, in certain respects. However, the institutions that were meant to keep things together proved to be weaker than the festivities suggested as Liberia battled complaints of corruption, growing costs, and street demonstrations in the years that followed. It is crucial to note that the nation did not return to war. However, the blue helmets' departure did not end the quiet process of reestablishing trust. Here, I should exercise caution. The closure in Somalia is a political mission, and UNMIL was a peacekeeping force with soldiers and police; the two are not the same. Liberia did not have an ongoing insurgency in 2018, but Somalia does. The lesson is still applicable, though. Three things to watch So where does Somalia stand? I'd say there are three things worth watching. The first is the election. The entire transition will appear to be successful if the major players agree to move on to the next round. We will soon learn the practical consequences of the UN's absence if it results in a disagreement over the regulations. The second is rights to humanity. In order to document abuses and speak out, journalists, activists, and displaced families depended on the mission. The government claims that national organizations can take over, and perhaps they can, but only if they are granted autonomy. It is not much of a commission if it is unable to hold the funders accountable. Thirdly, there is security. Al-Shabaab has not disappeared, and the African Union has not yet completed the transfer of security responsibilities. Weakness in the military and political disputes feed each other. Every time leaders engage in combat, the rebels gain ground. A test of ownership This does not imply that the choice was incorrect. A nation cannot continue to be governed by foreign powers indefinitely, and many Somalis were fed up with the idea that foreign powers controlled their politics. It makes sense to want to control your own destiny. Owning it, however, entails doing the difficult part, which entails making concessions, putting up with regulations that occasionally work against you, and creating institutions that outlive any one president. The UN is no longer involved in politics. We won't know for a few years whether that was courageous or premature. We do know that if the negotiations fail, no one else will be held accountable going forward. __________________________ Hussein Shegow Mohamed is a Somali writer and political and security analyst. He holds a Master’s degree in International Relations and Diplomacy and a Bachelor’s degree in International Relations. His work focuses on Somalia’s security, governance, and sustainable peace. somalia.content: Somalia’s Constitutional Test: Presidential power must answer to law - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Somalia’s Constitutional Test: Presidential power must answer to law Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Hirsi Abdulkadir Mohamed Sunday November 8, 2026 A constitutional limit means little if a president can respond to judicial scrutiny by replacing the leadership of the court examining his authority. That is the principle at stake in Somalia’s confrontation between the presidency and the judiciary. On 7 November 2026, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud attended the swearing-in of Ibrahim Idle Suleiman as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. He emphasized judicial independence, accountability and equal justice. Yet the circumstances surrounding the appointment raise a fundamental question: will the presidency accept those principles when they constrain its own power? Two days earlier, the Supreme Court reportedly ruled that the mandates of Somalia’s federal institutions had expired. It held that constitutional amendments increasing terms from four to five years did not automatically grant existing officeholders another year. The court directed political stakeholders to agree on an electoral framework within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, while limiting the government to routine administration. advertisements The dispute concerns more than the timing of an election. It tests whether Somalia’s constitutional institutions can impose meaningful limits on those who govern. Under Articles 60 and 91 of the 2012 Provisional Constitution, parliamentary and presidential terms were four years. Any claim to an additional year therefore depends on the legal effect of subsequent amendments, particularly their transitional provisions. Changing the length of future terms and extending an incumbent’s mandate are distinct legal acts. The latter requires a clear constitutional foundation because it changes the conditions under which authority was originally entrusted. Without that distinction, constitutional reform risks becoming a mechanism through which officeholders prolong their own rule. The ambition to introduce direct elections does not remove this obligation. Electoral reform must proceed through lawful institutions and procedures. Its democratic promise cannot, by itself, authorize an extension of power. The judicial leadership dispute makes the situation more serious. President Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed before the mandate ruling, citing concerns about the administration of justice. The Supreme Court subsequently declared the dismissal unconstitutional and accused the president of interfering with a pending constitutional case. The replacement’s swearing-in nevertheless proceeded. This sequence raises substantial concerns about executive interference, although timing alone does not establish personal motives. The presidency must explain the legal basis for removing the previous Chief Justice and appointing his successor while its own mandate is under judicial examination. Article 90(j) of the 2012 constitutional text connects presidential judicial appointments to recommendations from the Judicial Service Commission. Article 111A assigns that commission responsibilities concerning judicial recruitment and dismissal. The government should publish the relevant decrees and demonstrate compliance with the applicable framework, including any subsequent legal changes. A swearing-in ceremony cannot cure an appointment made without lawful authority. Nor does replacing a Chief Justice reverse an existing judgment. Any challenge to the court’s decision must follow an authorized legal process. The judiciary must also establish the basis of its authority. The 2012 constitutional framework assigns important constitutional functions to a distinct Constitutional Court. A complete assessment must therefore explain how the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Division acquired jurisdiction over this dispute, including through any applicable transitional legislation. The authenticated judgment, operative constitutional amendments and relevant judicial laws should be publicly accessible. Questions about jurisdiction or procedure deserve reasoned answers through lawful channels. They cannot simply become a justification for executive disregard. Meanwhile, Somalia must preserve essential public administration. Salaries, services and security responsibilities cannot be suspended while political leaders contest their mandates. But administrative continuity does not automatically preserve unrestricted presidential powers. If the reported caretaker limitations are legally effective, a consequential judicial appointment requires a specific legal justification. International partners should support transparency, judicial independence and an inclusive electoral settlement with clear deadlines. Their pursuit of stability must reinforce constitutional accountability. Accepting indefinite uncertainty over mandates would weaken the institutions on which lasting stability depends. Federal authorities, Federal Member States and opposition leaders must negotiate a credible electoral process while protecting peaceful political participation and the judiciary’s freedom to act. Political agreement can facilitate a lawful transition; it cannot permanently replace constitutional authority. President Mohamud has called for judicial independence. He should demonstrate that commitment by submitting his administration’s claimed mandate and judicial appointments to transparent legal scrutiny. The Constitution must bind the presidency when compliance carries a political cost. Otherwise, Somalia risks establishing a dangerous precedent: that those entrusted with power may decide for themselves when its limits apply. _________________________________ Hirsi Abdulkadir Mohamed is a lawyer and Horn of Africa political analyst. Photo courtesy of Egyptian Foreign Ministry. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty discussed Red Sea security and regional stability with his Somali and Djiboutian counterparts on Saturday, stressing that responsibility for the strategic waterway’s security and governance rests exclusively with countries bordering it. Abdelatty held separate meetings with Somali Foreign Minister Abdisalam Abdi Ali and Djiboutian Foreign Minister Abdoulkader Hussein Omar on the sidelines of the 22nd Ordinary Session of the Executive Council of the Community of Sahel-Saharan States (CEN-SAD) in Tripoli, Libya. advertisements During his meeting with Abdi Ali, Abdelatty discussed ways to strengthen bilateral relations and expand cooperation, particularly in the economic, development and investment sectors. He reaffirmed Egypt’s commitment to supporting efforts to build Somali state institutions and enhance their capabilities, reiterating Cairo’s firm support for Somalia’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as the preservation of its national institutions. Abdelatty also reiterated Egypt’s categorical rejection of any unilateral measures that could undermine Somalia’s territorial integrity or infringe on its sovereignty. The two ministers exchanged views on developments in the Horn of Africa, highlighting the importance of strengthening national institutions and preserving the unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of countries across the region. They also agreed to continue coordination and build on the outcomes of the consultative summit hosted by Egypt in El-Alamein in October, as part of broader efforts to promote peace, stability and development in the region. In his meeting with Djiboutian Foreign Minister Abdoulkader Hussein Omar, Abdelatty welcomed the two countries’ commitment to expanding bilateral cooperation, particularly in the political, economic and investment fields. Their discussions covered cooperation in energy, logistics, ports, maritime connectivity and infrastructure, as well as ways to increase trade and mutual investment. Abdelatty also highlighted the importance of technical cooperation and capacity-building programmes delivered by Egyptian institutions. On regional developments, the two ministers exchanged views on the latest political and security developments in the Horn of Africa, particularly in Sudan and Somalia, and efforts to promote regional peace and stability. Abdelatty underscored the importance of supporting national institutions and safeguarding the sovereignty and territorial integrity of countries in the region.
